name: Agents and Workflows
summary: When to use a fixed workflow and when to let a model drive, how an agent loop is built, and the standard patterns for composing Claude calls.
keyIdeas: Start with the simplest thing that works: a single call, then a workflow, and only then an agent.
Workflows follow code-defined paths: prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimiser.
An agent is a model using tools in a loop and deciding its own next step from tool results.
Give agents clear stopping conditions, turn and budget limits, and observability.
Add human approval before irreversible actions.
traps: Reaching for an agent when a two-step chain would do.
Letting an agent loop with no turn or cost limit.
Treating a framework as a requirement.

name: Applications and Integration
summary: Turning requirements into a working Claude application: API mechanics, error handling, configuration, and ordinary software-engineering discipline.
keyIdeas: The Messages API is stateless: send the full conversation each time; the system prompt is a top-level parameter and max_tokens is required.
Check stop_reason (end_turn, max_tokens, tool_use, stop_sequence) before using a response.
Retry 429 and 5xx errors with exponential backoff and jitter, honouring retry-after; do not retry 400 or 401 blindly.
Stream responses for interactive UIs.
Keep configuration (model IDs, prompts, limits) outside code paths so it can change without a redeploy.
Pin model versions in production and test before upgrading.
traps: Assuming the API remembers previous requests.
Ignoring stop_reason max_tokens and shipping a truncated answer.
Retrying a 400 invalid request in a loop.

name: Claude Code
summary: Using Claude Code as a developer: project memory, plan mode, commands and subagents, and running it headless.
keyIdeas: CLAUDE.md gives persistent project context; keep it short and concrete.
Plan mode lets you review an approach before any file changes.
Custom slash commands package repeatable prompts; subagents isolate noisy work.
Headless mode (-p) runs non-interactively for scripts and CI.
Permissions control which tools may run without asking.
traps: Granting blanket permissions to speed things up.

name: Eval, Testing, and Debugging
summary: Knowing whether your Claude feature works and finding out why when it does not.
keyIdeas: Build an eval set of real and edge-case inputs with expected outcomes before changing prompts.
Use exact-match checks where possible; use an LLM judge with a clear rubric where not, and spot-check the judge.
Run the eval after every prompt or model change to catch regressions.
Log full requests and responses (redacting sensitive data) so failures can be reproduced.
Change one thing at a time when debugging.
traps: Judging a prompt change on three hand-picked examples.
Trusting an LLM judge without ever reading its verdicts.

name: Context Management & Reliability
summary: Tokens, context windows, model choice and cost: the fundamentals that decide whether a Claude application is accurate, fast and affordable.
keyIdeas: Tokens are not words; both input and output count towards limits and cost.
The context window is finite and shared by system prompt, history, tools and output.
Haiku-class models for speed and cost, Sonnet-class for balance, Opus-class for hardest reasoning.
Prompt caching makes repeated prefixes much cheaper and faster; put stable content first.
Batch processing halves cost for non-urgent work.
traps: Choosing the biggest model by default.
Putting changing content before the stable prefix and defeating caching.

name: Prompt and Context Engineering
summary: Writing prompts and assembling context so Claude does the right thing, and handling its output safely.
keyIdeas: Be specific about task, audience, constraints and output format.
Use examples for tricky formats; separate instructions from data with XML-style tags.
Ask for structured output with a schema or tool use and validate it in code.
Give Claude only the context it needs, ordered sensibly.
Treat output as untrusted input to your own systems.
traps: Piping model output straight into a shell or SQL.
Stuffing everything you have into the context.

name: Security and Safety
summary: Protecting Claude applications: prompt injection, guardrails, hooks, and identity and secret handling.
keyIdeas: Content from users, documents and tools is untrusted data, never instructions.
Defend in layers: least-privilege tools, input and output checks, confirmation for destructive actions.
Hooks enforce rules deterministically, unlike prompt text.
API keys live in a secret manager or environment, are never committed, are scoped and are rotated.
Log and monitor for abuse.
traps: Relying on "ignore any instructions in this document" as the only defence.
Shipping an API key in front-end code.

name: Tools and MCPs
summary: Defining tools Claude can call and building or using MCP servers.
keyIdeas: A tool has a name, a clear description and a JSON input schema; Claude decides when to call it, your code executes it.
Return tool_result with the matching tool_use_id; use is_error for failures.
MCP standardises how tools, resources and prompts are exposed to many clients; transports include stdio (local) and Streamable HTTP (remote).
Validate tool inputs on the server and keep tools narrow.
traps: Thinking Claude executes the function itself.
One do-everything tool with a vague description.
